concept: Zone sharding for tiered hardware (hot, warm, cold)
summary: Source-anchored research for Zone sharding for tiered hardware (hot, warm, cold). Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Hot, warm, and cold are operator-defined zone names and hardware choices, not fixed MongoDB storage classes. MongoDB documents a fast recent tier and a slower archive tier; a third intermediate tier extends the same range-placement mechanism. (medium confidence)

Rolling retention tiers require an operator or automation to update absolute date boundaries. The balancer enforces the configured ranges; a fixed boundary does not advance merely because documents become older. Rotation frequency trades operational frequency against migration volume per rotation. (medium confidence)

To benefit from targeted reads, queries should include the relevant shard key or usable prefix. Queries without it can broadcast across shards, so a cold tier can remain part of an application read path even when most user-facing data is recent. (high confidence)

Configure zone placement before allowing newly added low-spec shards to receive ordinary balancing traffic. Percona warns that adding those shards with the balancer running can move unintended data; MongoDB's hardware-tier tutorial stops balancing while configuring zones. (high confidence)

A reported hot/cold configuration with shard key order {id, ts} used MinKey-to-MaxKey spans for id in both ranges and failed with an overlapping-zone-range error. This illustrates why a trailing timestamp cannot be treated as an independent age partition across every leading id. (medium confidence)

Zone configuration needs eligible destination shards. The balancer policy warns that chunks in a zone with no assigned shards cannot be balanced, so a tier label and its date ranges alone do not provision working cold capacity. (high confidence)

Age-based placement needs a shard key whose ordered ranges can distinguish the ages being separated. A creation-date prefix can support this; hashing the age field makes its zone ranges operate on hash values rather than chronological intervals. (high confidence)

Zone intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound, and cannot overlap. Derived ordering consequence: when the leading date and field names are equal, an upper bound ending in MaxKey sorts above a lower bound ending in MinKey. Those bounds leave an overlapping key interval rather than being the same adjacent boundary; use matching complete compound-key boundaries. (medium confidence)

Zone sharding maps shard-key ranges to named groups of shards. Assigning recent and archival ranges to shards with different hardware lets one collection serve data with different latency requirements. (high confidence)

Cold-shard economics depend on having substantial rarely accessed data and accepting slower reads for it. Smaller RAM and CPU allocations and slower, higher-capacity disks can reduce infrastructure cost, but these sources do not establish a generally applicable savings percentage. (high confidence)

Zone changes converge through chunk migrations. Existing chunks can violate the new placement rules until balancing completes, and migration activity can affect cluster performance; plan rotation timing and verify final placement. (high confidence)
Ranges outside all configured zones may reside on any shard. Cover the intended chronological domain explicitly if hot/warm/cold hardware placement must apply to all records. (high confidence)

A monotonically increasing timestamp used for range sharding can concentrate new writes on the highest-key chunk and its shard. Hardware tiering therefore does not by itself distribute concurrent new inserts across the hot shards. (high confidence)
